title: Va'etchanan: the right and the good (Deuteronomy 6:18)
hook: do "that which is right and good"; the rabbis read it as going beyond the letter of the law

segments.voice: Yesterday, Va'etchanan and the four places the Shema's words travel. Your line was at home and on the way. Today, the portion's last stop: a phrase that goes past the rules.

Porters are carrying a barrel of wine for a rabbi named Rabbah bar bar Chanan, and they drop it. The barrel breaks. The wine runs into the dirt. By the rules of the time, workers who broke what they carried could be held liable, so the rabbi takes their cloaks as security. The porters go to Rav and complain. The story is in the Talmud, and it's an uncomfortable one, because the rabbi with the broken barrel isn't exactly wrong. Today's phrase is what Rav tells him.
screen: `A BARREL OF WINE IN THE DIRT.` → `HE TAKES THEIR CLOAKS.` → `THEY GO TO RAV.`

segments.voice: Rav says: give them back their cloaks. Is that the law? the rabbi asks. Rav answers with a verse from Proverbs about walking in the way of good people. So he gives the cloaks back. Then the porters say: we're poor, we worked all day, we're hungry, and we have nothing. Rav says: pay them their wages. Is that the law? Yes, Rav says, and quotes the rest of the verse, about keeping the paths of the righteous. The story doesn't use the name, but later teachers reach for it to explain a phrase the Talmud uses elsewhere: lifnim mishurat hadin. Literally, inside the line of the law. Not breaking the law. Standing back from the edge of it, where you could legally stand, and choosing to give more. Where does it come from? One root is today's verse from Va'etchanan: "And thou shalt do that which is right and good in the sight of the LORD." The medieval teacher Nachmanides, the Ramban, explains it like this. The Torah can't list every situation between neighbors and business partners and friends. So after all the specific rules, it adds a general one. Do the right and the good. Compromise. Give way. Go further than the line. The Talmud makes the same point darkly elsewhere: it says Jerusalem was destroyed because people judged strictly by the letter of the law and never went beyond it. A society can follow every rule and still be hard.
screen: `GIVE BACK THEIR CLOAKS.` · `PAY THEM THEIR WAGES.` · `INSIDE THE LINE OF THE LAW.` · `THE RIGHT AND THE GOOD.` · then, large: `BEYOND THE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where you're entirely within your rights: a refund you could insist on, a fee someone owes you, a rule that lets you say no. You're not wrong; now picture Rav looking at it, and ask who's on the other side and what their day has been. Let one small step back from the line come to mind.
Lifnim. Inside: short for lifnim mishurat hadin, inside the line of the law, choosing to give more than the law requires because it's right and good.
Your line: beyond the letter. The right and the good asks more than any list of rules. Rest well.

screen: `DAY 491 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EIKEV: NOT BY BREAD ONLY (DEUTERONOMY 8:3).`

howItsDone: In Jewish ethics and law, acting lifnim mishurat hadin, beyond the letter of the law, is praised as the way of the pious, and some later authorities hold that a court may in certain cases press people to act this way.

fork.setup: you're Rabbah bar bar Chanan. your porters broke your wine barrel, and you've taken their cloaks. Rav hears the case. what does he tell you?

give back the cloaks, and pay their wages.

original.note: Hebrew: inside the line of the law. the rabbis' phrase for doing more than the law requires.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice, beyond the rules.

what a scholar hears: the Ramban on Deuteronomy 6:18 links the verse to compromise and lifnim mishurat hadin; Bava Metzia 83a tells the porters.

chat.says: If the law was on the rabbi's side, why did Rav tell him to pay the porters?
options: Do the right and the good: step back from the edge of the law.
Rav ruled that a rabbi must always pay double to keep a good name.
Rav thought the wine was cheap, so the loss didn't really matter.
chat.meaning: The lesson's phrase is lifnim mishurat hadin: standing back from what the law allows, to do the right and the good.

lifnim mishurat hadin.meaning: inside the line of the law: giving more than required
